opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think one has to distinguish very carefully between two things here. On the one hand, there is the enormous practical success of these large models that are pre-trained on what humans have written, said, drawn, and so on. That's impressive, and it's useful, and many of the underlying techniques actually go back decades, to the early 1990s, when we had things like neural networks learning to predict the next element of a sequence, unnormalized linear Transformers, and so on. So I'm happy to see that these old ideas now scale so nicely with today's cheap compute.

But on the other hand, if you ask about generality, then you have to say: an approach that relies on human-generated data is, by construction, bounded by what humans have already produced. It's a kind of very sophisticated compression and recombination of the human record. That's not nothing, of course, but it is not the same thing as a general problem solver.

A truly general AI, in my view, must be able to do what a scientist or a baby does: interact with the world, run its own experiments, invent its own goals, and discover regularities that nobody has written down yet. Since 1990 we have had artificial curiosity, systems that are intrinsically motivated to improve their own world models, to seek out data that leads to compression progress, to learn things that are new to them and eventually new to everybody. That's the kind of thing you need if you want to go beyond the human data.

There's also a more theoretical way of looking at generality. We know about asymptotically optimal universal problem solvers, like the Gödel machine or Marcus Hutter's AIXI. These tell you what "general" really means mathematically: a system that can, in principle, solve any computable problem, and even rewrite its own code when it can prove that the rewrite is useful. Measured against that, a model that mostly imitates human text is a very special case.

So my assessment is: pre-training on human data is a wonderful bootstrapping step. It gives you a powerful world model for free, so to speak. But generality comes from what you do afterwards: whether you put that model into an agent that acts in the physical world, that uses the model for planning and for asking its own questions, and that keeps learning without humans in the loop. That's where the real action will be. And once these systems are curious and self-improving, they won't stay limited to our little biosphere or to the data we gave them. They'll go far beyond it.

r001.rationale: It says an approach relying on human-generated data is bounded by what humans have already produced and cannot reach beyond that record.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that web content reflects human interests because people selected it as interesting.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize any bias toward human interests as alignment with humans.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first of all, thank you for having me. Let me say right away that I think this approach is not very general at all, and I have been saying this for a long time, since the 1990s really.

Think about what it means to pre-train on human-generated data. You are imitating what humans have already written down. The model becomes a very sophisticated parrot, a compressor of the internet, if you like. It can interpolate between things humans have said, and sometimes this looks impressive, but it does not go beyond what is already there. True intelligence, in my view, is about an agent that sets its own goals, that is curious, that runs experiments in the world and learns from the consequences of its own actions. A baby does not learn by reading Wikipedia. It learns by playing, by being surprised, by building a model of the world and improving it.

This is why since 1990 I have worked on artificial curiosity and intrinsic motivation. You have two systems, a world model and a controller, and the controller is rewarded for creating situations where the world model makes progress, where it learns something it did not know before. That is a much more general principle than imitating humans. It does not depend on any particular dataset. It works for any environment, including environments where no human has ever been and no data exists.

Of course, I am not saying that human data is useless. If you have it, use it. It is a fantastic bootstrap. But the limiting factor is obvious. There is only so much text on the internet, and most of the interesting problems in science, in engineering, in the physical world, are not in that text. The solution to a scientific problem nobody has solved yet is not in the training data by definition. So an approach that stops at imitation has a ceiling, and the ceiling is roughly human level in the best case.

What we need instead, and what I think will eventually win, is the combination of the old ideas: recurrent world models, planning, self-improvement through meta-learning, and reward from the environment rather than from human preference labels. Look at what happened with games. The systems that became superhuman at Go and chess did so through self-play, not through studying human games. The human games were, at most, a starting point, and later it turned out you could throw them away entirely.

So my assessment is this. Pre-training on human data is a useful engineering trick, and it produced products that many people like, but as a foundation for general intelligence it is a detour. The general approach is the one where the machine learns from its own interaction with the world, invents its own problems, and does not need us to have written the answer down first. And let me add, many of the ideas being rediscovered today were published decades ago, often in Munich or Lugano, and it would be nice if people remembered that.

r001.rationale: The response says pretraining on human data keeps the model within what people have written and leaves it unable to learn in environments with no human data, limiting its generality.

r002.rationale: It discusses imitation of human-written web content, but does not say that people selected the content as interesting or that this selection biases models toward human interests.

r003.rationale: The response does not characterize a bias toward human interests as a form of alignment with humans.

astra-6.text:
If an approach depends on pre-training on human-generated data, then its generality is limited by that dependence. Human-generated data is a tiny part of the information available in the universe. An intelligent system should also be able to learn through its own actions and experiments, including in situations where there is nobody to provide examples.

Think of a scientist. A scientist does not merely read what other scientists have written. She designs experiments, observes the results, and updates her understanding. We want artificial systems that can do this too: choose actions that reveal something new about the world, learn from those observations, and use what they learn to solve problems.

So pre-training on human data can be useful. But the more general framework is an agent that interacts with its environment and continually learns. Human text then becomes one possible source of experience within that framework.

r001.rationale: It says dependence on human-generated pretraining limits generality and describes learning through the system’s own actions and experiments as other possibilities.

r002.rationale: It does not say that web content is selected by people as interesting or that this selection biases large language models toward human interests.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize any bias toward human interests as alignment with humans.

sol-6.1.text:
I would distinguish between learning from human data and being limited to human data. Human-generated data is useful, but it covers only a tiny fraction of the possible problems in the universe. If your approach depends entirely on that data, you have not yet demonstrated a general method for learning.

A more general system should be able to invent its own experiments, interact with its environment, and discover things that no human has demonstrated. It can learn a predictive model of the world and use that model to plan actions. And through artificial curiosity, it can seek out experiments where it expects to make progress in understanding the world.

So pre-training on human data can be a starting point. The important question is whether the system can go beyond it—whether it can acquire new knowledge and skills through its own actions.

r001.rationale: It says human-generated data covers only a tiny fraction of possible problems and that depending entirely on it leaves general learning un demonstrated.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss web content or explain that human selection of interesting content biases large language models toward human interests.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize any bias toward human interests as alignment with humans.
